title: Baldwin
name: Baldwin
metaTitle: Baldwin 1031 Exchange Services in Jacksonville, FL
metaDescription: Baldwin 1031 exchange coordination for rail-served industrial land replacement property at the US 90/301 and CSX rail junction.

sections.html: Baldwin sits at the historic junction of US 90 and US 301 in west Duval County, a town that grew up around a CSX rail crossing predating most of Jacksonville's suburban growth, and its replacement-property scope reflects that rail-junction identity: small in scale, industrial and land-focused, and adjacent to but distinct from the larger Westside industrial submarket a few miles east.

sections.heading: Rail-Junction Industrial Scope
sections.html:
Baldwin's commercial and industrial base is small relative to the rest of Duval County, and the properties that do qualify as replacement candidates tend to be rail-served or rail-adjacent land, small-format warehouse buildings, and highway-frontage parcels along US 90 and US 301 rather than the larger big-box distribution product found closer to Cecil Commerce Center.

The town's population has stayed small for decades, and its commercial identity remains tied to the rail crossing rather than to any recent rooftop-driven retail growth, which keeps Baldwin's transaction volume genuinely limited compared with the rest of west Duval County.

sections.heading: Property Types
sections.html:
Baldwin's identification lists draw from the following narrow set of categories:

  • rail-served industrial land at the CSX junction
  • small-format warehouse buildings along US 90
  • highway-frontage retail and service buildings on US 301
  • agricultural and timber land with rail-adjacent access
  • truck terminal parcels serving the US 90/301 corridor

Rail-served industrial land carries the clearest premium of these categories for a buyer specifically seeking rail access, while the highway-frontage retail and service buildings trade closer to standard small-town commercial pricing without a meaningful rail-related premium attached.

sections.heading: US 90/301 and CSX Corridor Specifications
sections.html:
Highway frontage along US 90 and US 301 should be verified against current road classification and any planned Florida Department of Transportation improvements, since a corridor upgrade can materially change a parcel's access profile within a hold period. Building specifications on Baldwin's small-format warehouse stock vary widely, and clear height and dock configuration should be confirmed directly rather than assumed from comparable Westside product.

Timber and agricultural land near the junction is sometimes marketed with a future-industrial narrative attached, and a buyer should weigh that narrative against actual utility availability and access easements rather than the corridor's rail history alone.

Truck turning radius at the US 90/US 301 intersection itself is a frequent bottleneck for larger trailers, and a tenant dependent on full-size trailer access should have that route field-checked rather than approved from a map alone.

sections.heading: Rail-Served Site Diligence Items
sections.html:
Any parcel represented as rail-served should be reviewed for actual CSX spur agreements and easement documentation, since the historic junction's presence in Baldwin does not automatically extend service rights to every adjacent parcel. Environmental diligence should also account for the site's long industrial and rail history, since legacy rail-yard use can carry soil or groundwater considerations that a newer Westside parcel would not.

A Phase I environmental report should be commissioned as a standard submittal item on any Baldwin industrial parcel with documented rail-yard history, and any recognized environmental condition should be resolved or priced into the acquisition before the property is carried on a final identification list.

sections.heading: Sequencing With the Westside Industrial Submarket
sections.html:
Because Baldwin's inventory is limited and Westside's Cecil Commerce Center corridor sits close enough to share tenant demand, exchangers commonly carry a Westside identification alongside a Baldwin property as a backup, and lender familiarity with rail-served industrial collateral should be confirmed early given how differently that underwriting reads compared with standard truck-only distribution space.

Given the market's small size, buyers should expect a longer marketing and diligence period than a comparable Westside acquisition and should build that extra time into the exchange schedule rather than assume Baldwin trades at the same pace as the larger industrial submarkets nearby.

faqs.q: What makes Baldwin distinct from the nearby Westside industrial submarket?
faqs.a: Baldwin grew up around a historic US 90/US 301 and CSX rail junction and carries smaller-scale, rail-focused industrial land rather than the larger big-box distribution product concentrated closer to Cecil Commerce Center in Westside.

faqs.q: Does being near the Baldwin rail junction mean a parcel has rail service?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Actual CSX spur agreements and easement documentation should be confirmed for the specific parcel rather than assumed from the town's rail history, since spur rights are parcel-specific and are not conferred by proximity to the junction alone.

faqs.q: What environmental diligence is specific to Baldwin's older industrial parcels?
faqs.a: Legacy rail-yard and industrial use in this area can carry soil or groundwater considerations that a newer Westside parcel would not, so environmental review should account for the site's actual history, and a Phase I report should be commissioned even on parcels that appear undeveloped on the current site plan.

faqs.q: What backup submarket pairs with Baldwin?
faqs.a: Westside, particularly the Cecil Commerce Center corridor, sits close enough to share tenant demand and is the standard backup identification for a Baldwin property, and lenders are generally more familiar with that corridor's collateral than with Baldwin's smaller rail-junction stock.

faqs.q: How should highway frontage along US 90 and US 301 be evaluated?
faqs.a: Against current road classification and any planned Florida Department of Transportation improvements, since a corridor upgrade can materially change a parcel's access profile within a hold period, and a buyer should request the current five-year transportation improvement plan directly from the county or state rather than rely on informal knowledge of planned work.
